title: The Elite Illusion: Achievement Effects at Boston and New York Exam Schools
research_question: Do schools with higher-achieving and more racially advantaged peer groups causally improve students' academic achievement and post-secondary outcomes? Specifically, what are the effects of exposure to higher peer test scores and a smaller share of minority classmates on test scores (state assessments, PSAT, SAT, AP) and college enrollment and quality for marginal applicants to selective public secondary schools?
data_description: The study combines administrative records from the Boston Public Schools (1997–2009) and the New York City Department of Education (2004–2007 application cohorts). Boston data include student registration, demographics (race, sex, subsidized lunch, limited English proficiency, special education), Massachusetts Comprehensive Assessment System (MCAS) math, English, writing, and science scores (grades 3–8 and 10), exam school application records with preference rankings, ISEE scores, and school-specific composite rankings, plus College Board PSAT, SAT, and AP scores and National Student Clearinghouse college enrollment data. NYC data include enrollment/registration files, SHSAT-based application and assignment files, and Regents exam scores through 2009. The unit of observation is a student-applicant. The Boston analysis covers 7th-grade applicants (1997–2008) and 9th-grade applicants (2001–2007); the NYC sample covers 9th-grade applicants from 2004–2007. Test scores are standardized by subject, grade, and year.
institutional_context: Boston and New York City operate networks of selective public secondary schools whose admissions are determined by entrance examinations and, in Boston, an applicant composite combining ISEE scores and GPA. Boston has three exam schools spanning grades 7–12 (O'Bryant, Boston Latin Academy, and the elite Boston Latin School) that allocate seats via a student-proposing deferred acceptance algorithm using school-specific rankings. New York's three traditional exam schools (Brooklyn Tech, Bronx Science, Stuyvesant) admit 9th graders solely on the SHSAT through a serial-dictatorship assignment. These schools are heavily oversubscribed and feature dramatically higher peer achievement and substantially fewer black and Hispanic classmates than the surrounding public schools that unsuccessful applicants typically attend. Following 1999, Boston exam school admissions ceased using racial preferences. The progressive selectivity of these schools means that successful applicants at different cutoffs experience very different counterfactual schooling environments.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: RDD — treatment = students admitted to exam schools, control = students not admitted; cutoff = exam score threshold

key_variables.treatment: admission to an elite exam school
key_variables.control: students who applied but were not admitted
key_variables.outcome: standardized test scores and other educational outcomes

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The main finding is that attending elite exam schools has no significant causal effect on student achievement. Students who just miss the admission cutoff perform just as well as those who just gain admission, suggesting the selective appearance of these schools reflects the characteristics of admitted students rather than a school quality effect.
